Consult Summary:
- 45-year-old woman with 3–4 months of painful, cracked, itchy palmar dermatitis interfering with work; impression: likely contact dermatitis.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Soreness and cracked skin of the palms and fingers for ~3–4 months, now painful and preventing work.
- Symptom onset/duration/progression: Began 3–4 months ago after job change; gradually worsened to current painful, work-limiting state; off work for past 3 days.
- Associated symptoms: Intermittent itch; occasional bleeding when scratched; no systemic symptoms (no fever, nausea/vomiting, bowel or urinary symptoms); appetite maintained.
- Prior treatments/trial: E45 emollient — ineffective; took an unspecified oral antihistamine — ineffective.
- Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes.
- Current medications: Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Allergies: None reported.
- Occupational/social history: Works as a hotel housekeeper, frequent exposure to cleaning products; reports not always wearing gloves. Drinks a couple pints of alcohol per week. Non-smoker.
- Family history: Diabetes in family. No known family skin disease.

Examination:
- (no physical examination findings documented)
- Vitals: not documented.

Impression:
- Likely dermatitis / contact dermatitis related to occupational exposure to cleaning agents.

Plan:
- Assessment summary: Contact/occupational dermatitis suspected given history of cleaning-product exposure and new job; symptoms persistent despite basic emollient and antihistamine.
- Treatment provided/planned:
  - Topical steroid cream prescribed — name/dose/route/frequency not documented in transcript; prescription to be sent to patient’s pharmacy.
  - Stronger emollients recommended to apply approximately 3–4 times daily for the next couple of weeks — specific product/dose not documented.
- Advice:
  - Avoid triggers: wear protective gloves when cleaning (recommended at all times).
  - Return precautions: review in 1–2 weeks; return sooner if symptoms worsen, spread, or fail to improve (doctor advised 10–14 days minimum before expected improvement).
- Follow-up: If no improvement within ~1–2 weeks or if worsening, patient to re-present for further management.

Quality checks (always include at bottom of note, or fill document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No documented physical examination of the hands (appearance, extent, secondary infection signs).
  - No vital signs.
  - Specific names, doses, routes, and frequencies for prescribed topical steroid and emollients not documented.
  - Diabetes control information (recent glucose/HbA1c) not provided.
  - Complete medication reconciliation (other medications) not provided.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - None identified.
- Transcript quality comment:
  - Transcript generally clear with conversational filler; some brief interruptions and verbal fillers but clinically relevant information is extractable.
